title: Bulkheads and load shedding
description: Learn about bulkheads and load shedding patterns for fault isolation. Understand how to prevent cascading failures and protect system resources.

data.text: Bulkheads and load shedding are fault isolation patterns that prevent failures in one part of a system from cascading to others. Inspired by ship bulkheads that contain flooding, these patterns isolate failures and protect critical system resources.
Bulkheads isolate resources so that a failure in one component doesn't consume all available resources and affect other components.

items: Separate thread pools for different services
Connection pool limits per dependency
Resource quotas per tenant or feature
Prevents resource exhaustion in one area from affecting others
Enables graceful degradation rather than total failure

data.title: Ship Analogy
data.text: Like ship bulkheads that compartmentalize flooding, system bulkheads compartmentalize failures. If one compartment fails, others remain operational.

items.title: Thread Pool Bulkheads
items.description: Dedicated thread pools for different services. If one service is slow, it only consumes its own threads, not the entire pool.

items.title: Semaphore Bulkheads
items.description: Limit concurrent operations using semaphores. Simpler than thread pools but may still share resources.

items.title: Connection Pool Bulkheads
items.description: Separate connection pools for different databases or services. Prevents one noisy neighbor from consuming all connections.

items.title: Resource Quotas
items.description: CPU, memory, or request rate limits per tenant or feature. Ensures fair resource allocation.

data.text: Load shedding intentionally drops requests when the system is overloaded to prevent complete failure and protect critical functionality.

items: Drop low-priority requests first
Return errors quickly instead of queuing
Protect critical path functionality
Prevents system collapse under overload
Better partial service than total failure

data.title: Graceful Degradation
data.text: Load shedding enables graceful degradation. Non-critical features may fail while core functionality remains available.

items: Random sampling—drop a percentage of requests
Priority-based—drop low-priority requests first
Rate limiting—reject requests above threshold
Client-side shedding—reject based on client tier
Feature flags—disable non-critical features under load

data.text: Bulkheads and load shedding serve different but complementary purposes.

items: Use bulkheads when: You have multiple services sharing resources, one service could consume all resources, you need isolation between tenants or features
Use load shedding when: System is under sustained overload, you need to protect critical functionality, some requests can be safely dropped
Combine both: Bulkheads for isolation, load shedding for overload protection
Monitor resource utilization per bulkhead
Set appropriate limits based on capacity planning
Test failure scenarios to verify isolation
Document what gets shed and in what order
Alert when bulkheads are near capacity
Consider the cost of unused reserved resources

data.title: Capacity Planning
data.text: Bulkheads reserve resources, which means some capacity may go unused. Balance isolation with resource efficiency through careful planning.
